articles.title: Montreal did not build a stadium for the 2026 cycling championships; it turned the city itself into one
articles.summary: Montreal hosted the 2026 UCI Road World Championships without building a new stadium for the event.
articles.body: Montreal hosted the 2026 UCI Road World Championships without building a new stadium for the event. Instead, the city temporarily transformed its existing streets, parks, transport links and bridges into a huge sporting venue. Across 8 days, 13 championship events brought more than 1,000 riders from over 80 countries onto routes spread across Montreal and the surrounding Monteregie region. PropertyLabs reported the approach as a temporary conversion of public infrastructure rather than a conventional construction project. The result was a championship where the city itself became part of the venue.How Montreal turned city streets into the cycling championships venueThe main event site was established at the foot of Mount Royal along Avenue du Parc, between Avenue des Pins and Avenue du Mont-Royal. According to the City of Montreal, this section contained the start and finish lines for every race and also hosted the Bonjour Montreal Fan Village. It was closed to vehicles from 4 September until 4 October, allowing time for the installation and removal of the temporary facilities as well as the championships themselves.PropertyLabs noted that this made an ordinary piece of public space function like event real estate for about a month. The change was temporary, but it affected everyday activities around the area, including vehicle access, parking, deliveries, waste collection and movement around nearby properties. Rather than adding a permanent building to the city, the organisers changed how existing infrastructure was used.The championship route spread far beyond one central venueThe races were designed to make use of Montreal rather than keep the competition inside a single circuit. Cyclingnews reported that organisers deliberately wanted the championships to show more of the city and involve local residents. The revised course used Mount Royal as its central feature while also adding a section beyond the usual Grand Prix Cycliste de Montreal circuit.The elite races extended even further. Tourisme Montreal reported that the men's and women's road races began in Brossard and travelled through 8 municipalities in the Monteregie region before crossing the Samuel De Champlain Bridge into Montreal. From there, riders tackled the Mount Royal circuit before finishing on Avenue du Parc.That arrangement turned roads normally used for commuting and regional travel into sections of an international sporting course. The bridge itself became part of the competition for a short period, showing how the event relied on infrastructure that normally serves a completely different purpose.What changed for residents during the racesA city-wide venue also meant city-wide disruption. The City of Montreal said the championships affected streets in 7 boroughs and Westmount, with routes changing from day to day according to the event schedule. Fences were installed along race routes from the morning, while streets were generally reopened after events, apart from the main championship site.Parking restrictions were introduced along affected roads, with vehicles in restricted areas subject to towing. The city also provided information on alternative parking arrangements and changes to collection schedules in affected boroughs. Public information meetings were held in June to explain the planned closures, obstructions and transport changes to residents.Tourisme Montreal also warned that temporary road closures and public transport adjustments would affect several parts of the city during the championships.The temporary venue required more than barriers and road closuresThe scale of the operation was larger than simply putting barriers along a few streets. Cyclingnews reported that 36 kilometres of roads were due to be closed for the event, excluding sections outside the city. The championships included 6 road races, 6 time trials, a mixed relay and the UCI Congress, creating a much larger organisational task than Montreal's established Grand Prix events.The time trials introduced another challenge because organisers had not previously hosted that type of race during the Montreal Grand Prix. The courses were planned around the St Lawrence River, where the flatter terrain suited the format. Elite time trials also crossed the river twice, adding major transport infrastructure to the sporting layout.Why the city became part of the spectacleTourisme Montreal described the 2026 championships as the city's most significant sporting event since the 1976 Summer Olympics. The event was free for spectators and included 13 road races and time trials, with fan areas along the route. More than 1,000 athletes from over 80 countries were involved, supported by about 1,500 volunteers.The decision to use the city as the venue also connected the championships with Montreal's existing cycling identity. Tourisme Montreal noted that the city has hosted the Grand Prix Cycliste de Montreal since 2010 and has UCI Bike City status, reflecting its wider cycling infrastructure and culture.The approach also had a long history behind it. Cyclingnews reported that the idea of bringing the World Championships back to Montreal had been developing since the early years of the city's Grand Prix races. When Montreal decided in 2021 not to bid for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the cycling championship bid was already prepared and was submitted almost immediately.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, Michael and Susan Dell helped launch a Hurricane Harvey recovery fund; backed by their $42 million contribution, it helped repair or rebuild 3,740 homes over the following three years
articles.summary: When Hurricane Harvey struck the Texas coastline in August 2017, emergency aid reached communities hit by the storm.
articles.body: When Hurricane Harvey struck the Texas coastline in August 2017, emergency aid reached communities hit by the storm. But as immediate relief efforts slowed, the need for long-term recovery became clear. Dell founder Michael Dell and his wife, Susan Dell helped launch the Rebuild Texas Fund with the OneStar Foundation to support rebuilding efforts across affected communities. The Dell Foundation contributed $42 million to the fund, which eventually raised more than $100 million from over 33,000 donors. Over the next three years, the fund backed hundreds of projects focused on helping Texans rebuild homes, restore businesses, access health services and recover essential community resources after the hurricane.How much did the Rebuild Texas Fund raiseThe Rebuild Texas Fund raised more than $100 million, with contributions from over 33,000 donors. According to the Dell organisation, every dollar went to organisations working in communities affected by Hurricane Harvey. The fund focused on four areas: health and housing, education and childcare, workforce and transportation, and small businesses.How many homes were rebuilt after Hurricane HarveyDuring the three years following the hurricane, the fund supported 290 projects across 41 counties and reached 2.1 million Texans as stated on the Dell Organisation website. Housing was a major part of the recovery effort. The fund helped repair or rebuild 3,740 homes, supporting families dealing with the long-term effects of the disaster.The programme also helped 265,842 people receive health services and provided essential materials to 3,724 teachers.How did the Dell fund help Texas businessesThe recovery effort also focused on helping local businesses return to normal operations. According to the Dell organisation, 1,411 businesses reopened with support from the fund.Other projects included equipping emergency medical services teams with lifesaving tools and restoring community facilities, including a Little League field.The Rebuild Texas Fund was created after Harvey to address needs that remained after the initial emergency response ended. Its three-year effort supported community-led projects aimed at helping affected areas rebuild and recover.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Lionel Messi's foundation helped fund a €37 million childhood cancer centre in Barcelona; when it opened in 2022, the hospital gained capacity to see up to 400 new cancer cases a year
articles.summary: For all the stadiums, trophies and record books associated with Lionel Messi, some of the most lasting chapters of his Barcelona story were written far
articles.body: For all the stadiums, trophies and record books associated with Lionel Messi, some of the most lasting chapters of his Barcelona story were written far from the football pitch. One of them took shape through a project aimed at children facing cancer. The Leo Messi Foundation was among the organizations that helped bring the SJD Pediatric Cancer Center Barcelona to life, creating a specialist facility where treatment, research and family support could exist under one roof, states an online report on Bein Sports. Scroll down to read the details.From an idea to a landmark centreAccording to Bein Sports, the project was promoted by Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, with the Leo Messi Foundation involved before construction even began. Its early contribution helped finance the centre's architectural development and supported the launch of the fundraising campaign. The foundation later became one of the project's 10 founding donors. In October 2018, with €2.6 million still needed to reach the €30 million fundraising target required to secure construction, the Leo Messi Foundation and Stavros Niarchos Foundation stepped in to jointly provide the remaining amount the report adds.The centre eventually opened its doors in 2022, creating additional capacity to treat childhood cancer patients and allowing the hospital to attend to as many as 400 new cancer cases each year, claims the online report.A wider commitment to childrenThe Barcelona cancer centre fits into a charitable effort that Messi has built over many years. His foundation, established in 2007, has focused largely on projects benefiting children and teenagers living in vulnerable circumstances.His work with UNICEF has been another important part of that commitment. Messi became a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador in 2010 and has since supported initiatives involving education, health and child protection.In 2012, the Leo Messi Foundation contributed funding to the Sports for Peace programme in Colombia, which used sport to support young people living in communities affected by violence. Five years later, the foundation helped finance 20 prefabricated classrooms in Syria, enabling more than 1,600 children affected by conflict to return to school, the report also states.Taking the mission beyond BarcelonaMessi's move to Inter Miami added another chapter to that work. In 2025, the Inter Miami CF Foundation and UNICEF began a three-year partnership supporting educational programmes for children in Argentina, El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras and Mexico. Messi also contributed to the partnership through an unusual fundraising project. He selected his header against Manchester United in the 2009 Champions League final as his favourite career goal and worked with artist Refik Anadol to transform it into a digital artwork, A Goal in Life. Christie's later auctioned the piece for $1.87 million, with proceeds benefiting several nonprofit organizations, including initiatives connected to the Inter Miami-UNICEF partnership.A different kind of Barcelona legacyMessi's life away from football has also expanded into hospitality, real estate, gastronomy and other business ventures. Yet the SJD Pediatric Cancer Center represents a different dimension of that legacy. It was not a one-off gesture but a project that developed over years, from architectural planning and fundraising to the eventual opening of a dedicated childhood cancer centre. Long after Messi's playing days in Barcelona ended, the project left something tangible behind, a place built around children, families and the difficult fight against cancer.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas city will pay at least $175,000 after the SpaceX site it owns pumped 128 million gallons of groundwater above permitted limits over three years; the settlement includes monitoring payments for 25 years
articles.summary: The city of McGregor will pay $175,000 in penalties after SpaceX pumped 128 million gallons of groundwater beyond allowed limits from a city-owned well, leading to a long-term financial commitment and monitoring system.
articles.body: A groundwater dispute involving SpaceX’s sprawling Texas operations has left the city of McGregor facing at least $175,000 in penalties and a 25-year financial commitment after the company pumped 128 million gallons of groundwater above permitted limits from a well owned by the city, as per the The Waco Bridge.McGregor City Council approved a negotiated settlement with the Southern Trinity Groundwater Conservation District on Monday, allowing the city to avoid a potential district court battle over the groundwater violations.The city is responsible for the penalties because it owns the SpaceX site and the wells used by the company.Under the agreement, McGregor will make a one-time payment of $50,000 by November 1, followed by quarterly payments of $1,250 for the next 25 years. The payments will help fund a new groundwater monitoring system on the well used by SpaceX.The settlement also requires the city to make “reasonable efforts to obtain additional sources of water”.The groundwater district issued violation notices to both SpaceX and McGregor in each of the past three years over the pumping, which totalled 128 million gallons above the permitted amount.McGregor City Manager Kevin Evans said the city was satisfied with the settlement and that SpaceX had already reduced its groundwater consumption at the site.“Water will always be an issue. We’re working with SpaceX and everyone else in the industrial park to use less potable water,” Evans said.Evans said SpaceX is also working to reuse water at its McGregor location, while the city is exploring alternative sources. Those options include buying groundwater from other communities or obtaining water from Belton Lake through the Bluebonnet Water Supply Corp., which already serves McGregor residents.Evans said he expected the settlement to end the city's conflicts with the groundwater district.Dispute over how much water remainsThe settlement has also highlighted a disagreement over the long-term condition of the aquifer supplying the area.McGregor Mayor Jim Lilley said concerns about groundwater depletion were overstated.“There’s plenty of water in the aquifer,” Lilley said after Monday’s council meeting. He added that the latest overpumping showed there was still substantial water available.Rodney Kroll, president of the Southern Trinity Groundwater Conservation District, disputed that assessment.Kroll said studies of the Southern Trinity Aquifer indicate that it does not recharge. As groundwater is extracted, he said, the water level therefore continues to fall.“Our aquifer does not recharge,” Kroll said. “What that says ultimately is that the water level is going down annually, and some day, we’ll reach a point where there’s no (ground)water.”Kroll said that point could come within about 50 years.The countywide groundwater district was established in 2008 after state regulators determined that the area faced “critical” groundwater shortages in coming decades.Why McGregor is payingThe financial responsibility has also drawn criticism from residents who argue that SpaceX should bear the cost of the groundwater violations.McGregor resident Danny Campbell opposed the settlement at Monday's meeting, arguing that SpaceX was the main driver behind the excess pumping but was not responsible for the litigation, fees or legal costs.“SpaceX is the primary driver for overpumping these wells, and they're not responsible for the litigation, they're not responsible for the fees, and they're not responsible for the attorney's costs,” Campbell said. “They're not responsible for any of it, and every dollar that goes towards things like this is one dollar taken from our community.”Campbell said she had taken out a $1,200 full-page advertisement in the McGregor Mirror to draw attention to the violations and what she described as a lack of transparency in the city's handling of the issue.Evans said the settlement would not be paid from tax revenue. Instead, the city plans to use money from the sale of city property to cover the penalty.With SpaceX having already reduced its groundwater use and McGregor seeking alternative water sources, city officials expect the settlement to resolve the immediate dispute. But the 25-year monitoring commitment means the consequences of the groundwater overpumping will remain part of McGregor's water management for decades.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: An Estonian gravel-road test developed cracks within months; 10 years later, a company says its stabilised soil gained strength
articles.summary: A gravel-road stabilisation test carried out in Estonia in 2015 is being presented by StabilRoad Holding as a decade-long example of increasing material
articles.body: A gravel-road stabilisation test carried out in Estonia in 2015 is being presented by StabilRoad Holding as a decade-long example of increasing material strength. The company said in November 2025 that laboratory tests of core samples taken from the road every two years showed the compressive strength of the stabilised soil had increased by an average of 1.0 to 3.0 MPa over 10 years. However, the company’s online report does not provide baseline strength values, the number of samples or the testing procedure behind the 10-year comparison. Earlier research commissioned by Estonia’s Road Administration recorded transverse cracks in the same test area within weeks of stabilisation, as well as further defects during subsequent inspections.The 2015 test on road no. 24109The test was carried out in July 2015 on road no. 24109 Kõo–Kolga-Jaani, between kilometres 17.7 and 19.1, near Kolga-Jaani. A 2017 research report commissioned by the Estonian Road Administration said the road was divided into test sections of about 468 metres. One section used the InfraCrete soil-stabilisation material with cement, while another used M10+50 and LBS polymers with cement. The stabilised layer on the InfraCrete section was 30 cm thick. The report said a 1.5-times surface dressing was applied to half of the stabilised test sections in 2015, while the other half was initially left unsealed so that changes in the stabilised gravel layer could be monitored. The remaining part was repaired and surface-dressed in 2016.“The current StabilRoad project page describes the Kolga-Jaani project as having been carried out in July 2015. It says the road was later treated with bitumen emulsion and crushed stone in the second year, followed by a 4 cm asphalt layer in the fourth year.Earlier research recorded cracksThe 2017 Skepast&Puhkim report found that the InfraCrete section developed transverse cracks relatively soon after stabilisation. The report said the cracks appeared within about a month. By spring 2016, inspectors recorded 11 transverse cracks up to 5 mm wide, including three on the part that had already received surface dressing. The originally unsealed section also had areas of unevenness and small holes. By June 2017, the section remained drivable, but the originally unsealed portion was more uneven, and the test section still contained small holes and transverse cracks. The same report recorded the InfraCrete section’s elastic modulus at 569 MPa in 2015 and 596 MPa in 2016. Its comparison table also gave an average IRI roughness value of 3.06 mm/m for the section. The report also found that 5 tonnes of InfraCrete had been used, twice the planned quantity of 2.5 tonnes. It suggested that the difference may have resulted from a calculation error when the material was spread using a cement spreader.The Skepast&Puhkim report ultimately said the tested InfraCrete and cement stabilisation method was not suitable for constructing dust-free light pavements on low-volume roads when its operating costs and actual test results were taken into account. Its calculated 25-year discounted operating cost for the InfraCrete and cement treatment was €116,871 per kilometre, compared with €44,451 per kilometre for the surface-dressing alternative considered in the study.What the company says after 10 yearsStabilRoad Holding's November 2025 report presents a different picture of the section's longer-term condition. The company says it monitored the road for 10 years and took core samples every two years to assess changes in the compressive strength of the stabilised soil. According to the company, the strength increased by an average of 1.0 to 3.0 MPa over the decade. The company also says visual inspections found that the appearance of the stabilised road surface had remained unchanged from its original condition. Its project description says the section was surface-treated in the second year and received a 4 cm asphalt layer in the fourth year. StabilRoad further projects that the same level of stability and strength could persist for another 50 to 100 years.The 10-year result therefore comes from the company's own monitoring rather than the earlier Road Administration research programme. The online company report gives the reported increase of 1.0 to 3.0 MPa, but does not publish the baseline compressive-strength measurements, sample count or laboratory testing method needed to independently assess the magnitude of that increase. The earlier research, meanwhile, documents cracking during the first two years of the test. The two sets of records describe different stages of the same road experiment and measure different aspects of its performance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Did he know?’: Why Israel is rejecting an October 7 reckoning
articles.summary: The fixation on Netanyahu’s failures allows Israel to avoid confronting what it has done in Gaza.
articles.body:
As Israel prepares to mark three years since the October 7 attacks and with less than a month to go to parliamentary elections, one topic is dominating the electoral agenda.

Media reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by the United Arab Emirates before the attacks have put his alleged responsibility back in the spotlight.

“Did he know?” is the question on everyone’s lips.

Listening to the accusatory choir, one might think that Israeli society finally is acknowledging the real meaning of October 7. Yet the opposite is true.

Instead of giving a platform to a reckoning, the elections function to scapegoat Netanyahu for his alleged role in facilitating Hamas’s attack while absolving Israeli society and the Zionist movement of its collective responsibility for the preceding violence and ensuing genocidal aggression.

For example, it does not insist on investigating whether the “Hannibal Directive” was deployed as part of the Israeli military response on October 7 and whether it killed Israeli citizens and how many.

It does not scrutinise subsequent Israeli military operations or whether they put the Israeli hostages in danger or how many were killed by Israeli bombs.

There is no questioning of why key Palestinian negotiators were attacked during ceasefire and hostage negotiations, including Ismail Haniyeh, Hamas’s chief negotiator, in July 2024 in Tehran and Hamas’s negotiating delegation in September 2025 in Doha.

There is no debate about why the Israeli government repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals that could have brought the hostages back much earlier.

There is little attention paid to the fact that Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant face arrest warrants from the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity.

The answer lies in the psychological state of Israeli society. For many Israelis, October 7 became a psychological rupture, making it difficult to reconcile their sense of humanity with their complicity in the criminal reality that followed.

The problem, then, is not that Israelis are in denial or misinformed. It is that a large portion of the society is complicit in criminality and actively avoids reckoning with it.

The absence of Gaza and Palestinians more broadly from Israeli political discourse is because of their complete dehumanisation by Israeli society.

How else could one explain the absence from the election rhetoric of questions about, and subsequent accountability for, actions against the Palestinian people?

Why has the Israeli military killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, the vast majority of them civilians? Why has it carried out mass and arbitrary detentions, torture and enforced disappearances of Palestinians?

Why has it targeted journalists , medical workers and academics ? Destroyed and occupied hospitals ? Wiped out ancient landmarks and irreplaceable cultural heritage sites ?

Why has the sadistic and often sexually deviant celebration of destruction, subjugation, ethnic cleansing and death by Israeli soldiers been allowed?

What’s more, there is also little interrogation of the consequences of bombing and invading Lebanon, killing nearly 9,000 people since October 2023. Or bombing Syria and Yemen.

These are not isolated abuses. They are symptoms of a system of theft and domination driven by greed and sustained through psychological conditioning, segregation, fear and rewards for aggression. In line with the “ Wired to Steal” model , dehumanisation helps produce consent for aggression while escalation following acts of resistance leads to normalisation of further expansion and robbery.

Thus, this election is not about a reckoning with October 7 or its horrifying aftermath. It is a lens onto a fascistic settler society engaged in denial and dehumanisation of an Indigenous “other” as a means of evading and normalising its own ongoing genocidal actions. Although Netanyahu may become the scapegoat, replacing him does not address the underlying machinery of domination and may instead serve to entrench it further.

That machinery remains firmly in place. The continuity between the violence unleashed since October 7 and the longer history of Zionist colonial expansionism is striking, with no lessons learned other than how to improve and grease the machinations of genocide. Fear, victimhood and the construction of a permanently besieged “us” against a dehumanised “them” continue to produce consent for further aggression and expansion.

October 7, therefore, has become not an occasion for genuine reckoning but another means of avoiding one. Netanyahu seeks to focus responsibility for the attacks on questions of what he knew and when while leaving the much broader record of what Israel has done since largely outside the electoral debate. His opponents, meanwhile, have their own complicity and ambitions to answer for. Thus, there is little political interest in a genuine reckoning with October 7. The fixation on Netanyahu allows the wider political establishment and Israeli society to avoid confronting the system of domination in which they remain invested.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: In 1993, Maryland used 60,000 tons of coal fly ash under a Route 213 overpass; later groundwater testing found no discernible impact at the site
articles.summary: In 1993, Maryland applied 60,000 tons of coal fly ash for the Route 213 overpass construction. Subsequent groundwater tests revealed no negative effects, showcasing fly ash's potential in infrastructure.
articles.body: Maryland used about 60,000 tons of Class F coal fly ash in 1993 and 1994, to build highway embankments for the Route 213 overpass over Route 301 on Maryland's Eastern Shore. The material came from Baltimore Gas and Electric and Delmarva Power plants, and several years later, state researchers tested groundwater around the embankment and found no discernible impact on groundwater quality at the site.Ash beneath the highwayThe fly ash was used as structural fill for the highway embankments near Centreville, and Maryland's Power Plant Research Program later studied the site as part of a state effort to examine the use of coal combustion products in construction. A base of silty sand was placed first, followed by sandy-clay berms along the sides of the fly ash. The ash itself was placed and compacted in 8-inch lifts. The fly ash was moistened to about 20% before compaction, and the finished fill was covered with two feet of sandy clay. Sections beneath the roadway received a stone base and asphalt pavement.A Maryland Department of the Environment fact sheet lists about 60,000 tons of fly ash at the U.S. Route 50/MD 213 overpass in Centreville, with about 40,000 tons coming from Delmarva Power's Indian River plant in southern Delaware and about 20,000 tons coming from the Brandon Shores Power Plant that was operated by Baltimore Gas and Electric.What happened underground?The Maryland Department of Natural Resources Power Plant Research Program began a field study at the site in March 1999, where researchers installed lysimeters and monitored wells and soil-moisture probes in and beneath the fly ash fill. Samples were collected from pore water and groundwater, which the researchers tested for dissolved trace elements, major ions and other chemical indicators.The EPA's case study reported that trace elements and major ions were present at elevated concentrations in the pore water inside the fly ash fill, which indicated that leachate was forming within the material. The groundwater beneath the embankment was different, where the data showed that the constituents were being attenuated in the underlying soil and groundwater. The groundwater measurements collected in May, June and July 1999 showed no discernible impact on groundwater quality at the site.A monitored highway embankmentFly ash could be compacted into structural fill for highway embankments, which gave transportation agencies another material for large earthwork projects. The Federal Highway Administration's national records list the Maryland Route 213 project as a 1993 fly ash embankment application, with its database recording the project at 91,000 metric tons, which is equivalent to about 100,000 U.S. tons, a figure that differs from the 60,000 tons of Class F fly ash identified in the EPA case study for the 1993-94 work.The difference is important because the federal records appear to describe the project using a larger material quantity, while the EPA case study specifically identifies 60,000 tons of Class F fly ash supplied for the embankments. The Maryland environmental study continued to examine how water moved through the fill and surrounding soils, where researchers were particularly interested in whether constituents that were released within the ash could reach groundwater.The EPA's assessment found that the constituents measured in the fly ash pore water were being attenuated in the soil and groundwater beneath the embankments, and the groundwater data available from the 1999 sampling period showed no discernible impact at the site. The Route 213 overpass therefore became a documented field case involving both large-scale use of coal fly ash and detailed environmental monitoring. The ash was placed beneath a working highway, while researchers tracked its physical and chemical behavior around the embankment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Philippines arrests 244 suspects in online scam crackdown
articles.summary: Criminals accused of using Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) as cover for human trafficking, fraud, murder.
articles.body:
Philippine authorities have arrested more than 200 foreign workers, mostly Chinese, in their biggest crackdown this year on illegal offshore gaming operators.

The country’s Immigration Bureau reported late on Saturday that military and other law enforcement agencies had raided two addresses on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao on Friday. Criminal gangs are accused of using Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) as cover for various crimes.

The raid on one site resulted in the arrest of 110 Chinese citizens, two Cambodians and a Hong Kong resident, according to the bureau’s statement.

A further 131 foreign citizens were arrested at the second site. Again, the majority were Chinese, alongside citizens of Malaysia, Indonesia and Myanmar, according to the statement.

Authorities seized large quantities of computer equipment, mobile phones, laptops and SIM cards.

Manila banned POGOs in 2024 on the grounds that crime groups use them as a cover for human trafficking , money laundering, kidnappings, fraud and murder.

A 2023 United Nations report noted that in recent years hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked by gangs and forced to work in scam centres and other illegal online operations across Southeast Asia.

The UN report estimated that at least 120,000 people across Myanmar and approximately 100,000 in Cambodia may be trapped in scam operations, with other criminal-owned enterprises in Laos, the Philippines and Thailand ranging from crypto-fraud to online gambling.

The Philippine government is investigating potential human trafficking-related offences by several of those arrested in the latest raids, while the rest will be deported.

International concern has grown in recent years over similar scam operations in other Asian nations, where trafficking victims are tricked or coerced into promoting bogus cryptocurrency investments and other cons.

“We will continue to enforce our immigration laws against foreign nationals who violate the conditions of their stay and ensure that the Philippines is not used as a base for illegal activities,” immigration chief Joel Viado said in the statement.

Chinese embassy spokesperson Ji Lingpeng told the AFP news agency that they are “reaching out to the Philippine law enforcement agencies on the details of this case”.

“Chinese law prohibits any form of gambling , including Chinese nationals gambling overseas or working for gambling companies,” he added.

articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Supreme Court protesters target Chief Justice Roberts’ vacation home
articles.summary: Liberal protesters in kayaks descended on Chief Justice John Roberts' Maine vacation home, continuing a pattern of targeting conservative justices.
articles.body: There are certain dates that have become a regular feature in American life. In February, the sandhill cranes return to the Platte River in Tennessee. In March, the swallows return to San Juan Capistrano. In October, the protesters returned to Hupper Island, the summer vacation home of Chief Justice John Roberts. The last migratory pattern is more recent and certainly less welcomed. In past years, liberal protesters have descended on the homes of conservative Supreme Court justices to disrupt their lives, shout abuses and, in one case involving Justice Brett Kavanaugh, seek to kill a member of the court. Protesters outside the home of Justice Amy Coney Barrett left bloody dolls on the lawn, knowing that she had young children inside. This week, protesters appeared at the vacation home of Roberts in Maine. Calling themselves "kayak-tivists," they formed flotillas facing his home to hold up signs and voice their displeasure at the jurist. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE It is an ironic moment for a chief justice, who has been regularly attacked by President Donald Trump for voting against his position in major cases ranging from tariffs to birthright citizenship. However, this is about rage, not reason. Back in 2022, Becca Shaw Glaser wrote about how Mainers needed to harass Roberts whenever he ventured out of his home. She wrote: SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES "Roberts is one of the most powerful people in the entire world. He comes to Maine to unwind and feel good about himself and his decisions, despite if he has just gutted our rights, forcing rape victims to give birth after an arbitrary time period determined by the government, gutted environmental protections, overruled basic gun regulations, decreed against the separation of church and state, and made politics much more unequal and infested with money.Exactly why should we continue to let Roberts use Maine as his easygoing backdrop for fun and relaxation? Why should Roberts get to breathe in the beautiful Maine air when he is fine with destroying methods of keeping our air clean?... Maine is not here as your happy place, your wind-down from all of your hard work destroying my civil liberties and democracy. No. May you never feel welcome here again." AMY CONEY BARRETT RECALLS HEARTBREAKING QUESTION FROM 12-YEAR-OLD SON OVER BULLETPROOF VEST Glaser, who was later dropped as a columnist, has pushed Mainers to hound Roberts wherever he goes in Maine: "Should you see Chief Justice John Roberts duck into Squid Ink coffee or the Port Clyde General Store this summer, consider letting him know exactly what you think of him and his illegitimate, ultra-conservative court. Yell, boo, whisper, weep audibly, give him the thumbs down or the finger, hand him a note, refuse to serve him." In its recent discussion of these protesters, the New York Times features Glaser and reveals how last year Glaser was approached by Roberts’ daughter, Josephine, who sought to defend her father during one of Glaser’s harassing protests. The Times recounts how liberals have been pushed to the breaking point by Roberts, despite the fact that he has had to curtail his movement around the island. WHAT'S NEXT IN THE BATTLE TO 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' AFTER SCOTUS RULING — AND THE HIDDEN DAMAGE DRIVING IT One of the featured suffering locals is Wendy Schlotterbeck, who was outraged when Roberts was spotted celebrating the Fourth of July on the island. The Times sympathetically explains the outrage since "[Roberts] and his colleagues had just narrowed protections for transgender athletes and minors and allowed Trump’s immigration crackdown to proceed." It recounts how Schlotterbeck has transgender relatives and "immigrant friends of hers [have] been arrested." Outraged, she left the picnic and, the next day, joined the "kayak-tivists" outside Roberts’ home. Protesting outside the home of a Supreme Court justice is a crime, though some of us have questioned the constitutionality of such laws. Putting that debate aside, the protests should be condemned by all Americans as reckless and wrong. JOHN YOO: BARRETT AND KAGAN’S SAFETY PLEA EXPOSES THE LEFT’S WAR ON THE SUPREME COURT Justices may hold different views on the left or the right, but they are all people of good faith who are trying to protect what they consider the essential rights of our Republic. Liberal justices have largely been spared such protests at their homes, though occasional protests have occurred. What is maddening is that this court has continued to show its independence in ruling with the law, rather than a partisan agenda. Unlike those on the left, who want to pack the court with an instant liberal majority in the name of fighting partisanship, the court continues to vote overwhelmingly on a unanimous or nearly unanimous basis. The conservative majority also continues to rule against the Trump administration when the law requires it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This term has many potential blockbuster decisions and the protesters are expected to return to the homes of justices around Washington. We have every right to debate, and indeed protest, such decisions. However, we should all unite around all of these justices — on the left and the right — in denouncing these protesters literally bobbing and floating on a sea of rage.

articles.title: Adam Copeland conquers Steve Maclin in highly anticipated match during Maple Leaf Pro's Northern Rising
articles.summary: Adam Copeland speared Steve Maclin through the ropes in a brutal street fight main event at Maple Leaf Gardens during Northern Rising night.
articles.body: Adam Copeland got one more chance to chase a dream on Saturday night as Maple Leaf Pro Wrestling (MLP) held Northern Rising at the venue known as Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto. Copeland had been open about his desire to perform at the facility. He previously spoke to OutKick Dropkick about it, noting that he watched his first pro wrestling match there when he was a kid. He didn’t get a chance to compete there when he was in WWE because the company had moved shows to a bigger arena as it grew in popularity. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE But Maple Leaf Wrestling and All Elite Wrestling (AEW) opened the door for Copeland to step foot inside an MLP ring. His opponent? Oh, just one of the hottest pro wrestling free agents on the market in Steve Maclin. The U.S. Marine-turned-wrestler had been champing at the bit to get to Copeland, even appearing on AEW "Dynamite" to blindside his opponent in the weeks leading up to Northern Rising. There was nowhere to run Saturday night. Copeland, Maclin go toe-to-toe in street fight Any normal 52-year-old man or woman probably shouldn’t be doing the things Copeland did in his street fight against Maclin in the main event of Northern Rising. Copeland going above and beyond to put on a show for those in Toronto underscored his legendary status in pro wrestling. Copeland suplexed Maclin from the ring apron in between a ladder that was propped upside down near the ropes. He also hit a big splash from the top turnbuckle onto Maclin, who was sent crashing through a table that was set up outside of the ring. Maclin doled out his fair share of punishment, too – suplexing Copeland onto a ladder. There were plenty of "Oh s---!" moments during the match. Maclin’s wife, Ring of Honor pure women’s champion Deonna Purrazzo, interfered and sprayed Copeland and the referee in the face. Fellow pro wrestling legend Rhino evened the odds. He speared Maclin and Purrazzo, helping the fight reset. Copeland would get back the upper hand. He stepped outside of the ring, onto the ramp and walked all the way up it before turning back around, sprinting down the aisle and spearing Maclin through the ropes. He hit one more spear before covering Maclin for the win. The Canadian superstar gave Maclin his flowers after the match as he addressed the crowd and spoke about how special it was to compete at Maple Leaf Gardens. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Undisputed MLP Canadian champion crowned Josh Alexander and Stu Grayson battled for the Undisputed MLP Canadian Championship ahead of Copeland’s match with Maclin. It was one of the matches of the night. Grayson came into the bout as the interim champion while Alexander considered himself to be the champion after never losing the title. He had only been out of MLP action because of a knee injury. When he returned, Alexander set his sights on Grayson. The feud needed to come to an end. Alexander would do his best to avoid any major moves from Grayson early. When Grayson went to the top rope, Alexander pushed him off and caused his opponent to crash onto several security members. In a high-stakes match, high-risk moves became common. Grayson was trying to get back his momentum and superplexed Alexander before nailing him with a knee to the face. Grayson couldn’t get the pin and it would be the theme for the rest of the match. Alexander would get help from Don Callis in the latter moments of the match. Callis jumped onto the apron with a screwdriver, but the referee appeared to thwart an attempt to hand the screwdriver to Alexander. Still, somehow, Alexander got his hand on the weapon and used it against Grayson without the referee seeing it. He then hit two C4 piledrivers and pinned Grayson for the win. Champions remain The Northern Rising card featured two more singles titles on the line. Priscilla Kelly defending her MLP Canadian Women’s Championship against Nikki Storm and Andrade El Idolo defending the AEW National Championship against Rohan Raja. Kelly appeared to have no interest in letting Storm take over the match. She seemed to be in control from the get-go. She nailed a dropkick on Storm as Storm was on the mat and leaning on the bottom rope. Kelly then went to work with her own myriad of kicks to Storm that turned into a stomp on her back. Storm had no answers for Kelly, who retained the title. Kelly has held the title for over 55 days as she won the belt in September on Maple Leaf Pro Wrestling "Mayhem" over Gisele Shaw. Meanwhile, Andrade was looking to settle the score against Raja, who has taken out several Luchadores on "Mayhem" over the last few weeks. Andrade is considered to be one of the best pro wrestlers in the sport, but Raja gave him all he could handle. Andrade’s prowess in the ring took over Raja’s innate abilities. Andrade, at one point, powerslammed Raja from the ring apron down to the floor. Raja put up a good fight, but it was Andrade who was still the national champion before the night was finished. Andrade shook Raja’s hand after the match, signaling that Raja was someone to watch. New champions take over 1st Faction was going to have a tough test at Northern Rising. Brent Banks and Sheldon Jean put the MLP Canadian Tag Team Championship on the line against Grizzled Young Veterans and Sinner & Saints. articles.title: Researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
articles.summary: Russian authorities are responding to an incident in which a dangerous infection was released as a result of a laboratory accident in Siberia and a researcher died.
articles.body: Russian authorities are responding to an incident in which a suspected dangerous infection was released as a result of a laboratory accident in Siberia and a researcher died. The incident occurred at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, near Irkutsk, according to Russian state media TASS. It is unclear exactly what was released, according to the state agency that handles infectious disease, Rospotrebnadzor. One person – a laboratory worker – is said to have died in the incident after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin. “The sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is stable,” Rospotrebnadzor said. Special measures had been carried out “in connection with the case of an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute,” Rospotrebnadzor said, adding that the employee had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” or cause. The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee – a 28-year old woman – died “possibly from the plague.” He also noted that “there are no plague outbreaks” in Buryatia. The governor of Irkutsk, Igor Kobzev, urged calm on Friday, saying that an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission was held with Russia’s chief state doctor. The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region,” Kobzev said on Telegram. An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, also urged calm and noted that “there are many rumors and conflicting reports circulating.” “All identified close contacts are under medical supervision. At present, they show no signs of the disease, and their laboratory test results are negative,” Fominikh said. Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, say that nearly 200 people were placed under observation at the hospital in Shelekhov to which the laboratory technician was taken. Quarantine has also been imposed in at least one of the city’s maternity hospitals, according to Liudi Baikala. The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a previous head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday. Onishchenko told the state news agency TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission. Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues. But the pneumonic plague, or lung-based plague, can transfer easily from person to person through respiratory particles. Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The World Health Organization has noted that plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics and the use of precautions to prevent infections.

articles.title: Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFP
articles.summary: Trucks were ‘clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles’, UN agency says.
articles.body:
An air strike on United Nations trucks has killed a driver in Sudan’s South Kordofan, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

The WFP said in a statement released on Sunday that the trucks, carrying food aid, were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles” as they came under attack. The agency did not identify those responsible.

The strike hit the convoy on Saturday as it was travelling between two cities controlled by the government’s Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in South Kordofan state.

Fighting in the Kordofan region intensified in late 2025, turning the territory into a strategic battleground between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The two have been fighting for control of Sudan in a civil war that has now lasted more than three years .

The extent of the damage and additional details regarding the attack on WFP aid trucks are still being assessed. The UN agency said that it has called for an investigation.

“These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need,” the statement reads.

Since the war began in April 2023, one in five attacks in Sudan has occurred in the Kordofan region. The army has the upper hand in the north, having made a series of recent gains , while the RSF maintains control over much of the west. South Kordofan remains contested.

Both the SAF and RSF have increasingly deployed drones in their war, with attacks on towns in North Kordofan growing more frequent and deadly, and civilian infrastructure coming under attack across the region.

The civil war has forcibly displaced 14 million people, plunging the country into one of the worst modern food crises and killing tens of thousands of people.

Nearly 19.5 million people – about 41 percent of Sudan’s population – were struggling with acute food crises between February and May, according to an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification assessment, a leading authority on global hunger. More than five million faced extreme, life-threatening food shortages, and 135,000 were at risk of famine.

articles.title: Search for 6 aboard medical jet enters second day after crash near Nantucket
articles.summary: Authorities on Sunday declined to speculate on what caused a medical evacuation jet to crash off the coast of Nantucket on Saturday morning, as crews continue to search for the six missing passengers.
articles.body: Authorities on Sunday declined to speculate on what caused a medical evacuation jet to crash off the coast of Nantucket on Saturday morning, as crews continue to search for the six missing passengers. Rear Adm. Matt Lake, commander of the Coast Guard’s Northeast District, said at a news conference Sunday that Coast Guard crews, Massachusetts authorities and the New York National Guard’s air rescue wing have searched roughly 2,840 square miles over more than 53 hours. “This is a large and demanding search area. Our crews are employing fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters to search the area,” Lake said. He added that authorities hope to use sonar to search the seabed. He declined to say whether the mission had shifted from rescue to recovery, which would mean no survivors are expected. He also declined to provide the passengers’ names or ages “out of respect to the families and next of kin.” The U.S. Coast Guard launched a search Saturday morning and found a debris field approximately 20 miles off the coast of Massachusetts’ Nantucket island later that day. Air traffic controllers lost contact with the jet early Saturday as it flew from Bermuda to Boston. One controller asked the crew whether it was declaring an emergency and “coming in blind,” according to audio obtained by NBC News. The six people on board were four Canadians and two Bermudians. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News the Bermudians were a patient and the patient’s son. The Bermudian government said Saturday that it was in contact with the families of those on board. The Coast Guard said it had notified next of kin. The flight was scheduled to last less than two hours, according to data from FlightAware, a site that tracks flights in real time. The jet took off from L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda at about 12:40 a.m. and was due to land at Boston Logan International Airport just before 1:30 a.m. Bermuda is a British overseas territory in the North Atlantic, about 775 miles from Boston. At around 1:05 a.m., FlightAware shows the jet dropping from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet over the Atlantic Ocean. The plane was operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, an Ontario, Canada-based medical evacuation company that arranges private flights for sick or injured patients. According to the company’s website, a typical flight is staffed by two pilots and two medical crew members and carries a patient and an escort. The Gulfstream jet that crashed Saturday was equipped to carry full ICU medical equipment and supplies. Lake said Sunday that investigators would likely try to locate the plane’s flight recorder system, or “black box,” which is designed to preserve evidence after a crash. “There’s no indications that we found a black box. But again, it’s very difficult because that debris is extensive,” Lake said.

articles.title: Council challenges Sleaford Beacon Fen solar farm approval
articles.summary: The Beacon Fen Energy Park was approved by the government in August.
articles.body:
A Reform UK government would try to prevent solar farms from connecting to the national grid, the party's deputy leader said.

Richard Tice, MP for Boston and Skegness, spoke as Lincolnshire County Council said it had launched a judicial review of a decision to approve a solar farm in the county.

The authority said the impact of the Beacon Fen Energy Park near Sleaford, which was approved by the government in August, may not have been fully considered.

A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson said the climate crisis was the biggest threat to agriculture and nature, and solar was among the cheapest and quickest forms of energy to build.

The Beacon Fen solar farm will be capable of powering up to 130,000 homes.

In August, the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero said there was an "urgent need" for the proposed development.

At a press conference on Friday, Tice said: "I'm announcing that a Reform government, very quickly after an election, will do all we possibly can legislatively to stop the national grid from connecting up these solar farms.

"So, my message to these overseas investors, caveat emptor [buyer beware]: you might lose all your dough, think very seriously about this."

County council leader Sean Matthews said the judicial review could cost up to £300,000, but he thought the authority had a good chance of winning.

The council said it had raised concerns throughout the planning process that insufficient weight may have been given to the impact of the development on communities, farmland and the cumulative effects of several other major solar developments in Lincolnshire.

"I will do what I can to stop these crazy solar farms, and I will do everything that I can to achieve that," Matthews said.

"And yes, if that means opposing all of these and putting judicial review against all of the solar farms that we've been told we're getting, then I will do that," he said.

In May, Lincolnshire County Council and North Kesteven District Council launched a claim for a judicial review to the High Court over the government's decision to approve plans for Springwell Solar Farm , between Lincoln and Sleaford.

Judicial reviews are court proceedings which look into the lawfulness of a decision or action made by a public body, the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary says.

A government spokesperson said it would not comment on individual projects, but all solar farms were subject to a rigorous planning process in which the views and interests of local communities were considered. This included any impact on biodiversity, visual amenity, or the natural environment.

"We continue to work with NESO [National Energy System Operator] on delivering the Strategic Spatial Energy Plan (SSEP) which will set out a strategy for how new infrastructure should be spread across the country," the spokesperson said.

The BBC has contacted Beacon Fen Energy Park for comment.

articles.title: Iran did not collapse after Khamenei — it just became harder to read
articles.summary: Six months after the deaths of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and Ali Larijani, Iran has transitioned into an opaque, security-centered governance model where authority is increasingly mediated by institutional decrees rather than centralized personal leadership.
articles.body:
Six months after the killings of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and Ali Larijani , the Islamic Republic has neither rebuilt the centralized hierarchy once concentrated around the supreme leader nor fallen into chaos. It has entered a more opaque second phase of rule: coercive institutions still function, but authority is more insulated, more mediated by security bodies, and harder to translate into reliable control across every theater.

Mojtaba Khamenei holds the formal office of supreme leader, and major appointments continue to be issued in his name. But the public evidence does not show him exercising the visible, personalized authority associated with his father. The result is a more security‑centered Iran, one in which outsiders can no longer safely infer how tightly the center controls the timing, escalation and interpretation of actions across every front.

Mojtaba has not made an independently confirmed public appearance since taking office, and no authenticated video or audio of him speaking after his appointment has been released. On Aug. 10, President Masoud Pezeshkian said he had spent about seven hours with Mojtaba in a meeting that has not been independently documented. Formal authority has continued to be exercised through institutions: A decree issued in Mojtaba’s name designated Mohsen Rezaei as the supreme leader’s representative to the Supreme National Security Council, after which Pezeshkian appointed Rezaei as secretary. On the same day, Hossein Taeb — a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence chief described by analysts as close to Mojtaba — was appointed Basij commander by a decree issued in the supreme leader’s name.

Leadership decapitation, a damaged command structure, economic siege, and regional pressure did not produce collapse. They produced a surviving system in which the security services and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are now the most visible and central wartime institutions.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps did not disappear into chaos. It became more central to the state’s survival, but not necessarily a more transparent or frictionless command system. Senior command losses and scattered proxy theaters, together with the opacity of wartime decision‑making, have left outsiders with evidence of more discretion and less visibility into who authorizes what.

Uneven behavior across Hormuz, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen does not necessarily prove autonomous regional commands. It may reflect distinct local constraints, proxy‑specific capabilities, deniability requirements, selective or delayed guidance, wartime delegation, and reduced outside visibility into the command process.

The result is a system of delegated coercion shaped by broadly understood Iranian guidance: Tehran’s strategic intent may remain broad, but the specific authorization, timing and calibration of local action are harder to infer. The public evidence does not establish proxy rebellion. The more supportable immediate concern is delegated escalation — partners pursuing overlapping objectives understanding guidance that can preserve deniability while making restraint and de‑escalation harder to verify.

Iran’s post‑decapitation system now points toward three plausible trajectories:

Security consolidation. Mojtaba retains formal authority while a small and fanatical leadership restores coherent command. Indicators would include consistent cross‑theater signaling, appointments that produce a durable and visible chain of command, and a negotiating channel capable of delivering compliance.

Insulated security equilibrium — the current baseline . Mojtaba remains unseen; key institutions mediate decisions; coercion is delegated; escalation is uneven. This resembles the present pattern: secrecy, selective escalation and security appointments that have restored a wartime center of gravity without restoring Ali Khamenei’s personalist command.

Fragmentation under pressure. Economic stress and military losses produce open elite disputes, uncontrollable proxy actions, or contradictory orders. This would require visible defections, intra‑elite conflict, or a sustained loss of internal‑security control.

Iran has survived decapitation through a more opaque, security‑centered system and more delegated coercion. That does not make it a failed state or a federation of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders. It just makes the Islamic Republic harder to read.

For Washington and regional capitals, the lesson is not that Tehran has lost control of its allies. It is that deterrence and diplomacy can no longer be judged chiefly by statements issued from Tehran. A message from Mojtaba’s office, an action in Hormuz, and a proxy escalation in Yemen may still serve the same broad strategy — but they cannot automatically be treated as evidence of a single, timely, and centrally calibrated decision.

Iran has neither restored its old order nor disintegrated into chaos. It is surviving through an opaque, security‑centered system whose authority remains formal at the top, but whose coercion is now harder to read and more delegated in practice.

Charbel A. Antoun is a Washington-based journalist and writer specializing in U.S. foreign policy, with a focus on the Middle East and North Africa.

articles.title: In 1974, Houston replaced most of an asphalt road base with incinerator ash; 3 years later, the 89% waste mix was performing almost like conventional pavement
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking project in 1974, Houston utilized incinerator ash in road construction, achieving impressive performance results that paved the way for sustainable, waste-based materials in infrastructure. Discover how this early experiment transformed urban road-building practices and addressed waste disposal challenges.
articles.body: In 1974, Houston, Texas, tried an unusual material for road construction: ash left behind after municipal waste was burned. Instead of sending the residue to landfill, engineers used it in an asphalt concrete base course on a city street. Three years later, the experimental section was reported to be performing almost like a conventional asphalt pavement. According to the US Department of Transportation’s ROSA P. collection, the project was an early example of turning a difficult waste stream into a construction material. The mix contained 89% incinerator ash, 9% asphalt and 2% lime by weight, meaning that most of the material in the experimental road base came from waste rather than newly quarried aggregate.A road base made largely from wasteIn the Houston experiment, engineers used littercrete, a stabilised asphalt material in which incinerator waste replaced much of the conventional aggregate. The experimental and control sections were laid on a municipal street, with an asphaltic layer placed over the base. After three years of traffic, a 1977 study compared the littercrete section with a conventional hot-mixed asphaltic concrete base, known as blackbase. Researchers assessed the road through field observations and tests on core samples taken from the pavement.The results were encouraging. The littercrete section was reported to be performing well and was described as almost identical in appearance and performance to the conventional control section. The report's reference to an 89 per cent waste content described the composition of the littercrete mixture by weight.What happened after three years?This project was part of a broader effort to find a use for the ash left behind when municipal waste was burned. Incineration reduced the amount of waste going to landfill, but it also created a new problem: what to do with the ash. Road construction seemed like a practical option because asphalt mixtures already required large amounts of aggregate.A later Federal Highway Administration review recorded several projects that tested municipal waste combustor ash in roads. In Houston's 1974 project, the aggregate used in a six-inch road base consisted entirely of incinerator ash. The littercrete mixture itself was different. By total mixture weight, it contained 89 per cent incinerator ash, 9 per cent asphalt and 2 per cent lime. Another Houston project in 1977 used a road-base mixture containing 70 per cent ash.These projects showed that incinerator ash could be used in road construction rather than simply being sent for disposal. However, they were still demonstration projects, so they did not establish that ash could replace conventional road materials on a large scale. They were early attempts to turn a waste product from incineration into a useful construction material.An early lesson in waste-based constructionHowever, what made the Houston road project noteworthy was that it showed an asphalt base containing a large proportion of incinerator ash could remain serviceable for several years under traffic. Environmental concerns were also part of the discussion. Municipal waste incinerator ash can contain soluble salts and trace metals, making proper processing and testing important before it is considered for construction use. Historical FHWA reports on the use of incinerator ash in construction identified advantages such as high stability and low unit weight, but those findings related to the projects and assessments of that period rather than a current recommendation for the unrestricted use of municipal waste incinerator ash.A study in the Journal of Cleaner Production found that the performance of asphalt mixtures containing municipal solid waste incinerator bottom ash depended on factors such as ash porosity and replacement rate. Higher ash contents could reduce high-temperature rutting resistance, while certain ash characteristics could improve moisture and low-temperature performance. Thus, the test Houston carried out in 1974 is located in an interesting position within the chronology of circular construction. The test suggests that waste material, which had hitherto been thought of as a waste product fit only to be disposed of in the incinerator, can actually be used to construct functional roads. The test does not present a method for building such roads, but it demonstrates their feasibility.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Flydubai hijacking attempt exposes worrying gaps in aviation security
articles.summary: The quick-thinking actions of the captain of last week’s Flydubai flight bound for Israel prevented what could have been an unmitigated hijacking disaster. But aviation safety experts say the incident raises serious concerns about the security failures before the flight and how it happened in the first place.
articles.body: The quick-thinking actions of the captain of last week’s Flydubai flight bound for Israel prevented what could have been an unmitigated hijacking disaster. But aviation safety experts say the incident raises serious concerns about the security failures before the flight and how it happened in the first place. The suspected attacker, named as co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, was removed from Oman’s national airline last year following concerns about his extremist views, sources told CNN. Both the United Arab Emirates and Israel have strict aviation security regulations – yet al-Hammami was allowed to fly. “A lot of the post 9/11 security measures that were adopted were meant to prevent an external threat – loading bombs or things onto an aircraft, you know, preventing a threat from amongst the passenger base from getting access to cockpits,” said CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas. “It wasn’t really designed with the theory that a pilot would do something like that.” There is no international standard for background checks. Experts said pilots’ licenses and security passes are handled at the national level, and the rules vary depending on the country. Questions about background checks in aviation industry The allegations of extremist views and the suspected attacker’s dismissal from a previous job have raised concerns about the reliability of background checks in the aviation industry. CNN has reached out to Oman Air, the Dubai government’s media office and Dubai Airports Company for comment. Flydubai said it could not provide comment while the incident remained under investigation. All flight crew members require an “airside” pass, which allows them to go to the non-passenger side of airports and aircraft, according to aviation expert Alastair Rosenschein, who worked as a pilot in the United Kingdom for four decades. Those passes typically require police checks and background checks to obtain, but experts say the process comes down to each country’s regulations. The Israeli Ministry of Transport told reporters on Saturday that it relies on foreign air carriers’ commitment to international regulations, as well as signed declarations that each carrier’s pilots and crews have been vetted. Rosenschein said that he doesn’t have insight into the specific process in the UAE, but “I do know where the responsibility lies, and that is with the government, with the airlines, and with security services – because no one else has the authority to investigate or pass on this information.” “There’s not really anything cast in stone as to how people are vetted – and there should be,” Rosenschein said, and questioned: “Why did the Omanis not suspend his pilot’s license?” Aviation expert and British pilot Gideon Ewers noted that a pilot’s license is essentially just a technical qualification that shows someone knows how to fly a plane. The license itself doesn’t come with a record of previous employment issues or infractions. Questions about hiring practices and ongoing checks Hiring practices also vary greatly by each airline, but most involve some sort of psychological evaluation, flight simulation tests and references from previous employers or trainers, Rosenschein said. Pilots must also pass regular medical exams. It’s unclear how the attacking pilot would have passed a referencing process if he was dismissed from the Omani airline for concerns about his extremist views. “The hiring process at company ‘A’ can be quite different from the process at company ‘B,’ even though it’s a similar role,” Ewers told CNN. “Any pilot who’s involved in the recruitment will say their primary question is asking themselves, ‘Would I want to sit in a cockpit with this guy for 12 hours?’” Rosenschein added that the main way airlines know if somebody is unfit to work is through internal company reporting. He said that “if somebody is acting strangely – maybe they started drinking heavily on night stops, etc. – they should be reported by their colleagues.” He argued that this attempted hijacking, as well as previous cases of pilot suicide-murders, show that much more needs to be done in terms of industry staff checks, including information sharing between airlines and countries, social media checks, random staff checks for substances like alcohol and regular psychological exams. None of that is standard across the industry. “I think that we have to move to a far more serious regulation in the industry because so many lives are at stake in an aircraft,” Rosenschein said, although he noted that flying today is far safer than when he began working as a pilot in the 1970s. CNN reached out to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency that helps countries cooperate on aviation matters, which said standards are “under continuous review by ICAO and are enhanced as ICAO identifies emerging priorities and new best practices.” A weapon on the flight deck On Saturday the UAE cleared up suggestions the suspect smuggled in a knife by confirming he used the cockpit’s crash ax, something found on most passenger planes in case an emergency requires breaking out of a damaged aircraft or breaking open panels to reach a fire. “You have a weapon on the flight deck. Should that remain there? I don’t think it should,” Rosenschein said, adding that the ax also presents security issues related to those outside the cockpit, as the door is sometimes opened during flights for bathroom breaks. It’s a difficult balance for airlines, which are tasked with preventing both accidental and malicious emergencies, as well as internal and external threats. For security, cockpit doors are locked from the inside, and experts say most planes are fitted with a switch on the control panel that can open that hard door. It’s unclear in the Flydubai incident if that’s how the injured Indian pilot opened the door to allow passengers to help. Some planes are also outfitted with emergency entry door codes, to allow access to the flight deck in the event of incapacitation of the crew, such as a pilot having a heart attack or stroke. But that would be unlikely to help in the event of any pilot-intended incident, such as an attack or pilot suicide. Investigations ongoing The United Arab Emirates and Israel are both investigating the incident, according to officials. There will also be an investigation conducted in Saudi Arabia, where the flight was diverted for its emergency landing. Saudi Arabia has no formal diplomatic ties with Israel. In the coming days, investigators will likely explore the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder first, said Marco Chan, a senior lecturer in aviation operations at London’s Kingston University. They will likely be digging further into the attacker’s medical history and training history, Chan told CNN. Investigators will also likely interview the other crew members, passengers and the off-duty pilots who managed to safely land the plane, he said. One Israeli official told CNN it is not yet clear how the Omani pilot would have obtained clearance to fly to Israel, given that Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations. Israel’s Tax Authority confirmed the names of all passengers and crew were in the hands of Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, but it said questions about the vetting of crew members should be referred to the Ministry of Transport. Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, also referred CNN to the Ministry of Transport, which it said is “responsible for all security matters concerning foreign airlines.” The Ministry of Transport said that its procedures do not include checking the names of flight crew members, although those names are submitted to the Israel Tax Authority, which collects them in case of requests by security services. The ministry added that all flight crew members are required to have a travel visa to enter the country, and an Omani passport should have been flagged at check-in. But the ministry also said its “procedures do not address the threat from a pilot.” On Sunday evening, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed the head of the country’s National Security Council to carry out a “thorough examination” of all aspects of the security of foreign civil aviation coming into Israel. When it comes to broader aviation hiring practices and background checks, security experts said those checks should theoretically be applied to everybody, regardless of nationality.
