articles.title: Cornell rape accuser faces threats demanding she drop her lawsuit, attorney says
articles.summary: The woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity members has received threats pressuring her to drop her lawsuit, her attorney said Sunday.
articles.body: The woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity members has received threats pressuring her to drop her lawsuit, her attorney said Sunday. Thomas Giuffra told CNN’s “State of the Union” that people attempting to unmask his client’s identity had also targeted at least three women mistakenly identified as her. The former Cornell student is identified as Jane Doe in court documents. “She’s received multiple threats, and women who aren’t even Jane Doe receive threats,” Giuffra said. He added that he had received a threat Sunday morning. Giuffra did not identify those responsible or say whether the threats had been reported to law enforcement. He did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for more information about the threats. Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month against Cornell and seven Chi Phi fraternity members, alleging she was sexually assaulted over the course of hours on Oct. 19-20, 2024, while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana. The allegations have sparked renewed scrutiny of the university’s and local authorities’ handling of the allegations. Gov. Kathy Hochul last week appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to consider whether criminal charges are appropriate. NBC News reported Friday that Cornell police interviewed witnesses and received anonymous tips during their investigation in 2024, but Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten did not review that additional information before deciding not to pursue charges at the time. He has defended his decision, saying that Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement to police did not allege criminality. Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday that the university must do better and that its board of trustees would announce an independent review of its handling of the case next week.

articles.title: A Romanian flea-market seller thought an old machine was a typewriter and let it go for €100; the buyer, a cryptography professor, recognized a World War II Enigma I and sold it at auction in 2017 for €45,000
articles.summary: A remarkable story of a cryptography professor who purchased a WWII Enigma I machine for €100 at a Romanian flea market, later selling it for €45,000 at auction, highlighting its historical significance and remarkable value.
articles.body: In 2017, a machine sold for €100 at a Romanian flea market turned out to be a German Enigma I used during World War II, after a cryptography professor recognised what the seller had mistaken for an ordinary typewriter. The rare machine later sold for €45,000 at an auction in Bucharest.The collector spotted the machine at a flea market and immediately recognised its significance. He bought it for €100 before eventually consigning it to Artmark, a Bucharest auction house.Artmark put the machine up for sale with a starting price of €9,000. It was eventually bought by an unnamed online bidder for €45,000.“The collector bought it from a flea market. He’s a cryptography professor and ... he knew very well what he was buying,” Cristian Gavrila, Artmark’s collectible consignment manager, told Reuters.The discovery was particularly significant because the machine was a German Wehrmacht Enigma I, a cipher device used to encrypt military communications during World War II.From a flea market to a €45,000 auctionThe machine had been made in Germany in 1941 and was described by an Artmark representative as being in almost perfect condition.Vlad Georgescu, a relationship manager at Artmark auction house told CNN, that collector had spent time cleaning and repairing the machine after buying it. He also said the previous owner had not realised what the object actually was and had believed it to be a conventional typewriter.The collector, described as a mathematician who had spent much of his life decrypting codes, began examining how the machine worked after acquiring it.Its eventual auction price was 450 times what the seller had received at the flea market.However, the €45,000 sale was not the highest price paid for an Enigma machine. A month earlier, a four-rotor Enigma cipher machine from 1944 had sold at Christie's in New York for $547,500, according to Reuters.Another Enigma machine featured in a Hollywood film about the Bletchley Park codebreakers had sold in London in 2011 for £133,250, as per the CNN.How the Enigma machine was usedThe Enigma was an electromechanical encryption device used by different branches of Nazi Germany’s military to encode and decode messages.Operators typed messages using the machine's keyboard. Its rotors could be set to different positions, changing the encryption produced by the device. Later versions also included a plugboard that added another layer of complexity.German forces believed messages protected by the system were difficult to decipher.That changed during World War II when British codebreakers at Bletchley Park worked to break the Enigma codes. Mathematician Alan Turing was part of the wider codebreaking effort.The work carried out by Turing and his colleagues is widely credited with helping shorten the war. articles.title: In 1994, Don Williams paid $1.35 million for 1.137 acres beside Maui's Maalaea Harbor; 32 years later, a Hawaii appeals court vacated a $7 million compensation judgment in the state's long-running eminent-domain fight
articles.summary: In August 1994, Don Howard Williams Jr. paid $1.35 million for roughly 1.137 acres of waterfront property beside Maui’s Maalaea Small Boat Harbor.
articles.body: In August 1994, Don Howard Williams Jr. paid $1.35 million for roughly 1.137 acres of waterfront property beside Maui’s Maalaea Small Boat Harbor. Four weeks later, he entered into a 30-year lease with the State of Hawaii.More than three decades later, that property remains at the center of a prolonged legal battle over how much the state should pay after seeking to take the land through eminent domain.On September 30, 2026, the Intermediate Court of Appeals of the State of Hawaii vacated a 2025 Circuit Court order and final judgment that had granted Williams’ motion for summary judgment and determined that he was entitled to $7 million in just compensation based on the evidence before the lower court, according to court document published on Justia.The appeals court did not rule that Williams was not entitled to compensation. Instead, it found that the Circuit Court had improperly excluded evidence from the state’s expert appraiser and had erred in resolving the valuation dispute through summary judgment while competing evidence remained.The case was sent back to the Circuit Court for further proceedings.A $1.35 million purchase becomes a decades-long legal fightWilliams purchased the Maalaea property on August 4, 1994, from FSO Oklahoma Investments Corp., an entity connected to the Church of Scientology’s Flag Service Organization.The land had a complicated ownership history stretching back more than a decade before Williams’ purchase.In the late 1970s, two of the parcels that eventually became part of Williams’ property were acquired by Maalaea Landing Inc., which planned to develop a condominium project there.The development plans never came to fruition. After financial difficulties, the property was transferred to Pioneer Federal in 1981. It subsequently changed hands through a series of transactions involving private investors, Oceanfront Associates and entities connected to the Church of Scientology.By 1992, FSO Oklahoma Investments Corp. had acquired the parcels that would eventually form part of Williams’ property.Williams bought the land for $1.35 million in August 1994.Four weeks later, on September 1, the State of Hawaii entered into a 30-year lease with him.The state initially agreed to pay rent for the propertyThe lease provided Williams with a long-term income stream from the waterfront property.State payments began at approximately $150,000 a year in 1994 and had increased to around $350,000 annually by 2013.The arrangement changed in June 2013, when the State filed a complaint seeking to condemn the property rather than continue making lease payments.The state said it sought the property in connection with improvements to the adjacent Maalaea Small Boat Harbor.That condemnation action transformed the property’s lease into a legal dispute over how its value should be calculated.The central question became whether the value of Williams’ interest in the existing lease should be taken into account when determining the compensation owed to him.The state’s position on the lease changedThe State of Hawaii initially argued that the value of the lease should be considered when determining just compensation.When the condemnation case was filed in 2013, the state deposited approximately $4.17 million based on its estimated compensation for the property.The state’s appraisal at the time included the land and the value of the lease.But the state later changed its position and argued that the lease income should not be presented to the jury when determining the property’s value.The dispute became especially important because the lease was producing hundreds of thousands of dollars annually.Williams argued that excluding the economic value of the lease could prevent him from receiving the full compensation required when private property is taken by the government.2018 agreement set compensation at $4.165 million - subject to appealIn June 2018, before trial, the parties entered into a stipulation agreeing that just compensation for the property was $4.165 million.However, Williams expressly retained the right to appeal earlier rulings in the case.The agreement also stated that the parties would remain bound by trial-court rulings that were not subsequently reversed or vacated by an appellate court.That provision became central to the latest appeals court decision.Earlier appeals court ruling reopened the valuation disputeThe case reached the Intermediate Court of Appeals previously.In April 2024, the appeals court ruled that the Circuit Court had abused its discretion by excluding evidence concerning the leased interest.The court held that evidence relating to possible future lease income could be presented in determining the property's value.The Hawaii Supreme Court later rejected applications from both the state and Williams seeking further review.The case then returned to the Circuit Court.Williams sought $7 million in compensationBack in the Circuit Court, Williams filed a motion for summary judgment in February 2025.He argued that the property interest he owned on June 27, 2013, the statutory valuation date, was worth $7 million.Williams relied on an appraisal by his expert, R.W. Spangler, and argued that the income-capitalization method was the appropriate way to value the leased property interest.The state filed its own motion for partial summary judgment in March 2025.It argued that the comparable-sales approach should be used instead.The Circuit Court ultimately granted Williams’ motion and denied the state’s motion.That decision led to the latest appeal.Appeals court says state’s expert evidence should have remained admissibleThe state raised three main arguments before the Intermediate Court of Appeals.It argued that the Circuit Court had wrongly granted summary judgment when material facts remained disputed, improperly excluded the state’s expert appraisal and wrongly determined that the income-capitalization method should be used instead of comparable sales.The appeals court agreed that the Circuit Court had erred.A key issue was the state’s expert, James Hallstrom.In earlier proceedings, the Circuit Court had ruled that Hallstrom could testify as a valuation witness for the state. That ruling had not been reversed or vacated.Under the parties’ 2018 stipulation, the appellate court said, Williams remained bound by that ruling.“Because the 2018 Stipulation bars Williams from arguing the Hallstrom report should be excluded, the Circuit Court erred by excluding it,” the appeals court ruled.The court said the competing valuations meant Williams’ motion had not established that there was no genuine issue of material fact.As a result, the Circuit Court should not have granted summary judgment in his favor.Court says there is no single valuation methodThe appeals court also addressed the dispute over how the property should be valued.Williams argued that the earlier appellate decision meant the income-capitalization method was controlling because the property had generated actual lease income.The state argued that comparable sales should be used.The appeals court said evidence based on income capitalization was admissible, but that did not make comparable-sales evidence automatically inadmissible.The court noted that the earlier decision had not established that comparable sales were invalid.“If an appraisal relied upon sales of similarly encumbered property, a jury could find the appraisal was reasonable,” the court said.Differences between the properties and their lease encumbrances, it added, would go to the weight of the evidence rather than its admissibility.Property had been sitting largely undevelopedThe legal battle has also drawn attention because of the property's location and its use.The Maalaea property sits beside the small boat harbor on Maui’s South Shore.Historical accounts describe the land as prime waterfront property that remained largely undeveloped for years.Williams had long been familiar with the area. He began visiting Maui in the 1970s and later lived in Maalaea, where he rented a condominium.He recalled regularly seeing the vacant property next to the Maalaea Mermaid and wondering why it had not been developed.When the land went up for sale in the early 1990s, Williams said he immediately saw an opportunity.He described the property as a “mini-Ilikai,” referring to the landmark Ilikai hotel in Honolulu.The lease became increasingly valuableWilliams’ lease with the state was structured around the market value of the waterfront property and prevailing rental rates in Maalaea.As property values increased, so did the state’s payments.The annual rent rose from approximately $150,000 when the lease began to around $350,000 by 2013.That income became the heart of the dispute over just compensation.Williams argued that the economic value of the lease represented an important component of what he owned when the state moved to condemn the property.The state eventually argued that the jury should instead focus on the value of the underlying property without separately considering the lease income.Condemnation triggered the valuation battleThe state's condemnation complaint was filed on June 27, 2013.The lease contained a provision under which the agreement would terminate if the property were condemned.The state therefore sought to acquire the land rather than continue making lease payments.But the question of what Williams was entitled to receive remained unresolved.The dispute has moved through the Circuit Court, the Intermediate Court of Appeals and the Hawaii Supreme Court system for years.The latest ruling does not settle the amount of compensation.Instead, it reopens the valuation process by requiring the Circuit Court to consider the evidence that had previously been excluded.What happens nextThe September 30 appeals court ruling vacated the Circuit Court’s April 2, 2025 order and July 9, 2025 final judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.That means the $7 million figure that Williams successfully obtained in the Circuit Court is no longer the operative final judgment.The lower court must now reconsider the case in light of the appellate ruling, including the competing appraisals and the permissible valuation methods.The income-capitalization approach can be considered because the property generated actual lease income, but the comparable-sales approach can also be presented.The ultimate amount of compensation remains unresolved.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two dead, 35 wounded in shooting at Georgia block party
articles.summary: Two people were killed and 35 others were wounded in a shooting at a block party early Sunday in south-central Georgia.
articles.body: Two people were killed and 35 others were wounded in a shooting at a block party early Sunday in south-central Georgia. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation said in a press release that shots were fired at about 1:25 a.m. in Vienna, a rural community about two hours south of Atlanta. Local station WALB News 10 described the event as a homecoming party. Dooly County Sheriff’s Office deputies were patrolling the party at the time, the bureau said. Two people were pronounced dead at the scene, and the wounded were taken to several regional hospitals. The bureau declined to say whether authorities had determined a motive or identified a suspect. “The investigation remains active and ongoing. At this time, no additional information is available for release,” Lydia Bullard, the bureau’s public affairs specialist, said in a statement to NBC News. Brett Watts, the Dooly County coroner, said the two people who died were both males, ages 20 and 23. Each had single gunshot wounds, Watts said, though an autopsy by the medical examiner’s office, scheduled for Friday, could provide a fuller picture. He said the men’s families have been notified.

articles.title: Early indications suggest Flydubai co-pilot acted alone in attack, officials say
articles.summary: Early indications suggest the Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain and trying to seize control of an Israel bound plane acted alone, rather than as part of a larger organization or on behalf of a foreign government, multiple U.S. officials briefed on the investigation and a former Israeli security official told NBC News.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — Early indications suggest the Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain and trying to seize control of an Israel-bound plane acted alone, rather than as part of a larger organization or on behalf of a foreign government, multiple U.S. officials briefed on the investigation and a former Israeli security official told NBC News. The U.S. officials cautioned that the investigation into Wednesday’s midair attack remains at an early stage. “The assessment is that he operated alone. Right now, it looks like a case of ‘lone wolf’ terrorism inspired by content found online,” said Shalom Ben Hanan, a former official in the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency. “We still need to wait for the final investigation results to determine whether an organization or a state is behind it,” he added. Emirati authorities, who are leading the investigation, said Saturday that the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash ax and attempted to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls in an attempted terrorist attack. The flight was carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv. A crash was averted when crew members and passengers entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker, according to eyewitnesses and Israeli officials. NBC News has identified the suspect as Omani citizen Hamam al-Hammami, based on information from multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East. Authorities have not released his identity. UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said Saturday that investigators were working to establish the incident’s “full circumstances, motives, and any links.” The preliminary assessment comes after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that investigators were examining whether the attacker had been sent by someone. President Donald Trump also raised the possibility of Iranian involvement Thursday, threatening renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack. A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation previously told NBC News there were no indications that Iran directed or was involved in the attack. The flight captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, said Friday from a hospital in Abu Dhabi that he had been severely injured and could sense the aircraft descending before he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene. “I was acting for my own life, but at the same time, I knew I couldn’t let all of them die,” he said on a video call released by India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Raf Sanchez and Paul Goldman reported from Tel Aviv. Tom Winter reported from New York.

A passenger on a rerouted flydubai flight that was bound for Tel Aviv said one of the pilots tried to crash the plane and kill everyone on board, after both pilots were found to be wounded on landing in Saudi Arabia. In the first comment by an official, Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir alleged an attempted "terrorist" attack in the incident, in which none of the passengers reported injuries.

articles.title: Oct 23 IAF air show event rescheduled due to MLC polls
articles.summary: IAF Varanasi air show reschedules Oct 23 event to Oct 24 due to MLC polls; 90-min aerial displays planned with major crowd, traffic and security measures.
articles.body: Varanasi: One of the three days of the proposed Indian Air Force (IAF) air show has been rescheduled, with the Oct 23 programme moved to Oct 24 due to the MLC elections for the teachers’ and graduates’ constituencies.Initially, the air show was proposed for Oct 22, 23 and 25. “But due to the MLC elections for the teachers’ and graduates’ constituencies slated for Oct 23, the show scheduled for that date has been rescheduled to Oct 24,” said divisional cmmissioner S Rajalingam.The air show is expected to feature around 90 minutes of aerial displays by various IAF aircraft, with nearly 30 lakh spectators likely to gather on both banks of the Ganga.Earlier, Rajalingam, police commissioner Mohit Agarwal, DIG Varanasi Range Vaibhav Krishna, District Magistrate Surendra Kumar, Chandauli SP Akash Patel and other officials conducted a field inspection of key locations ahead of the proposed grand air show. The inspection covered Padav, Ramnagar Bypass, Tengramor, Domri Ganga Ghat and Kodopur Ghat in Trans-Ganga. The officials reviewed the event area, spectator zones, approach routes, parking sites and security arrangements and issued detailed instructions to the concerned officials.The divisional commissioner directed officials to prepare a comprehensive crowd management plan by identifying potential pressure points in advance. Separate entry and exit routes, barricading, holding areas, queue management systems and designated pedestrian paths are to be ensured at major ghats and viewing points. Adequate police personnel will be deployed to regulate and divert crowds wherever required.To ensure smooth traffic movement, a detailed traffic plan, along with alternative routes and diversion arrangements, will be prepared and widely publicised. Vehicles will be allowed to park only at designated sites, while main roads, link roads and emergency routes must remain clear.Security along the riverbanks will be strengthened through coordination among the water police, local police and other agencies. Continuous monitoring through CCTV cameras, drones, control rooms, QRTs and response teams will be ensured. articles.title: Country star Ella Langley only wants one thing — and it's a big, 'beefy' whitetail buck
articles.summary: Ella Langley's old whitetail deer hunting clips resurfaced amid internet outrage over her harvest photos, but the country star has never hidden it.
articles.body: Ella Langley apparently has a very specific vision for her dream hunt. And, surprisingly enough, it does not involve anything exotic. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS In a resurfaced clip from CMA Fest 2024, the country star was asked what her dream hunt would look like. Her answer was pretty simple. "My dream would be a massive white tail," Langley said. When pressed for details, she got more specific. Langley said she wanted a big, "beefy" buck and would prefer to use a rifle, likely her .30-06 or .308 — the latter being a gun she said she has used to kill plenty of deer. She also joked that while she could do it with a bow, there is "a little more guessing game than a rifle." To recap: a big buck with a rifle. No need to overcomplicate things, right? The old clip has resurfaced at an interesting time for Langley, who recently found herself on the receiving end of some very predictable internet outrage over hunting. A few weeks ago, old photos of Langley posing with bucks she had harvested in Alabama started making the rounds again on social media. Critics acted as though they had uncovered some dark secret, despite the fact that Langley herself had posted the photos in the first place. Nothing says "caught red-handed" quite like finding publicly posted photos of someone openly doing the thing they openly enjoy doing. Ella Langley shares her biggest hunting regret Another older hunting clip, recently posted by the Porch Light Unfiltered page on Sept. 21, makes Ella's passion for the sport even more obvious. In that video, Langley was asked about her biggest hunting mistake or regret. Her answer was brutal. "The biggest deer I ever killed, I never found," she said, calling it "one of the hardest lessons I’ve ever learned deer hunting." RILEY GREEN FILLS THE FREEZER AFTER SCORING A MASSIVE BULL ELK WITH A BOW IN THE UTAH MOUNTAINS Langley explained that she shot the buck back in high school, just before she had to take the ACT. She got so excited that she moved too quickly to retrieve it instead of giving the deer enough time after the shot. She eventually realized she had jumped it, and despite searching with her dad, they never recovered the animal. She clearly still feels awful about it. "Oh, it haunts me," Langley said, adding that beyond losing the deer, the experience bothered her because taking an animal’s life is "a serious thing." That part probably does more to explain Langley as a hunter than any old photo ever could. She wasn’t mourning a missed mount for the wall. She was bothered by the fact that she had taken an animal’s life and never got the chance to recover it and harvest the meat — a responsibility she clearly doesn’t take lightly. Which makes the recent outrage over her old deer photos seem even sillier. Langley has never exactly hidden the fact that she hunts. The resurfaced clips only reinforce that. But she’s probably not losing sleep over people on the internet being mad about it. After all, her hit "Choosin’ Texas" has now spent 24 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, extending its record as the longest-running chart-topper in history. articles.title: NMC Seeks Rs748.62Cr Grant From State To Compensate For Entertainment Tax Waiver
articles.summary: Nagpur Municipal Corporation seeks Rs748.62 crore state grant to offset entertainment tax revenue loss after GST-era suspension and exemption extended to Sept 30, 2026.
articles.body: Nagpur: Cash-starved Nagpur Municipal Corporation (NMC) has once again initiated efforts to secure a Rs748.62 crore grant from the state govt to compensate for the revenue lost due to suspension of entertainment tax collection. The tax was suspended after GST implementation in 2017.Around three years ago, the then municipal commissioner Abhijeet Chaudhari had written letters to the govt seeking the grant. However, no concrete assurance was received. NMC has started the process for sending a fresh proposal to the govt as temporary exemption from entertainment tax collection ended on Sept 30.Before GST came into force, a special department under the district collector’s office collected entertainment tax. On May 29, 2017, the state govt amended the Maharashtra Entertainment Duty Act and transferred the power to collect the tax to local bodies. Subsequently, NMC started collecting entertainment tax from single-screen cinemas, multiplexes, cable connection operators and programmes organised at auditoriums and cultural halls, including ticketed social and cultural events.With implementation of GST from July 1, 2017, the state granted a temporary exemption from entertainment tax under Section 3 of the Maharashtra Entertainment Duty Act.The suspension resulted in a substantial loss of revenue for the civic body. The exemption, introduced in 2017, was extended by the state cabinet on May 3, 2023, under then chief minister Eknath Shinde, up to Sept 30, 2026.Before NMC, the district collectorate earned Rs20.24 crore from entertainment tax in 2015-16 and Rs24.01 crore in 2016-17. Had the collection continued, the annual revenue was projected to rise steadily over the years. As per the civic administration’s estimates, the potential annual revenue loss has risen to Rs148.80 crore in 2026-27.“Entertainment tax was a major source of revenue for NMC. The grant, if provided, would bring financial relief for the civic body and help overcome fund constraints for development works,” said Milind Meshram, officiating additional municipal commissioner.Year | Entertainment tax revenue2015-16 — Rs20.24 crore2016-17 — Rs24.01 crore2017-18 — Rs28.84 crore2018-19 — Rs34.61 crore2019-20 — Rs41.53 crore2020-21 — Rs49.83 crore2021-22 — Rs59.80 crore2022-23 — Rs71.76 crore2023-24 — Rs86.11 crore2024-25 — Rs103.34 crore2025-26 — Rs124.00 crore2026-27 — Rs148.80 croreYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Nagpur | Silver Rate in Nagpur | Bank Holidays in Nagpur | Public Holidays in Nagpur | Petrol Price in Nagpur | Diesel Price in Nagpur | CNG Price in Nagpur | LPG Price in NagpurStay updated with the latest Nagpur news. articles.title: Pro-Imran Khan mass rally launched after Pakistan government talks fail
articles.summary: Supporters of jailed former prime minister have set off from northwest Pakistan towards Islamabad.
articles.body:
Supporters of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan have set off on a protest march from the country’s northwest after talks with the government to call off the demonstration failed.

More than 5,000 were reported to have begun the rally on Sunday. The march, planned by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed until October 4 to allow talks between the government and the PTI leadership to take place.

However, two rounds of talks over the weekend failed to break the deadlock, and the PTI decided to carry out its plan, which is the latest attempt to pressure the government into releasing Khan, the country’s most popular political figure according to polls, who has been behind bars since August 2023 following a series of convictions that his party calls politically motivated.

All but one of the convictions against the former PM have since been suspended or overturned on appeal.

Videos posted on the PTI’s official social media showed supporters joining the march in different areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which is ruled by the party, and setting off in convoys.

Sohail Afridi , the region’s chief minister, had earlier posted on social media that the demonstration in support of Khan would go ahead.

He said the march will make its way to Khairabad, 80 kilometres (50 miles) west of Islamabad, by Thursday, where the plan for the “next phase” will be announced.

The government has been preparing for weeks for the arrival of PTI demonstrators in Islamabad. It has erected barriers using shipping containers to block main access routes to the capital.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi confirmed earlier on Sunday that the talks between the two sides had failed. He accused Afridi of “sabotaging” the negotiations, and added that the government would not allow the PTI to “create a disturbance”.

He also cited an Islamabad High Court order from September 14, ruling that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”.

“If they violate the orders, whether they are workers or politicians, whether they are protesting within KP or outside KP, we will pursue them one by one. This time, we want to ensure that these repeated episodes of creating disturbance in Islamabad come to an end,” Naqvi said.

Concerns about the 73-year-old Khan’s health, in particular the condition of his right eye that has required months of specialist treatment, have prompted the PTI’s campaign for his release.

The party has also called for the release of Khan’s three sisters, whose arrests last month further heightened tensions.

James Dorsey, a fellow at the National University of Singapore, said Khan was “essentially a populist leader” with “a genuine popular movement that had broad popular support”.

That is behind the “determination by the government to prevent [the protesters] from entering Islamabad,” he told the AFP news agency.

Given Pakistan’s security concerns, particularly following its unresolved February 2026 conflict with Afghanistan , Islamabad wants to avoid escalation in the face of the protests, he added.

“It’s a problem for the government, but I don’t think it’s an existential threat,” he said.
